2: To start: ARC is university robotics competition — drive, aim and fire at opponents’ armour panels to reduce hit points.
Established community: Purdue, NYU, McMaster, Queen’s, Ontario Tech and UBC — experienced teams to learn from.
Our choice: 1v1 Infantry — one robot, one pilot; manageable first-season scope.
Target: 2026–2027 season; roughly late June / early July 2027, based on past scheduling. Dates and venue unconfirmed.
3: From that interest, our first step: review the 2026 rulebook; next edition not yet available.
Chassis: 600 mm starting cube; 25 kg excluding referee hardware.
Power: voltage, battery-capacity and chassis-power limits; cutoff must isolate chassis motors from all power sources.
Launcher: one 17 mm launcher; maximum 25 m/s; illumination for fluorescent projectiles.
Referee system required, plus motion and firing qualification tests.
These constraints set the boundaries for our design.
4: Beyond the rules: choose a design achievable before competition — concrete enough to budget and assign work.
Pilot laptop → Type C control board → three robot functions.
Drive: four-wheel X-drive; sheet-metal chassis and spacers.
Aim: two-axis gimbal; two GM6020 motors for yaw and pitch.
Fire: motorized feeder supplying one 17 mm launcher.
Then vision assistance: OV9782 camera + Raspberry Pi 5 + Hailo AI HAT+.
Manual operation first; competing must not depend on finishing vision.
5: From the constraints and design: identify and price the required parts by subsystem.
Includes motors, electronics, referee hardware, charging equipment and materials.
Building is only part of the cost; next, getting to competition.
6: Beyond the robot: estimate attendance costs using Purdue’s 2026 venue; next venue unconfirmed.
Robot transport: 1,632 km × C$0.50/km = C$816. Rate quoted by Ryan Hammer.
Registration: approximately C$208; transport + registration ≈ C$1,024.
Base airfare: C$810 per person, kept separate as traveller numbers may change.
Planning total: approximately C$5,967 + C$810 per traveller.
Excluded: taxes, shipping, import duties, accommodation, meals and baggage.
Reprice travel when dates and venue are confirmed.
7: To meet those costs: lead our own fundraising, without drawing on UTRA’s existing funds.
Sponsor lead: Sable Metal — request sheet metal, laser cutting and forming; not yet confirmed.
Donations: drivetrain wheels already lined up; seek more parts and materials.
University funding: reviewed SEF and CPSIF criteria against our budget.
SEF: lasting equipment benefiting engineering students → referee hardware, chargers and vision hardware.
Reuse across future robots and member training gives UTRA a concrete equipment-funding case.
CPSIF: engineering engagement, inclusive participation and a justified budget.
Our case: motors, controllers and materials for hands-on design/testing, with open recruitment.
Value to UTRA: a costed project and application evidence; ARC leads the fundraising work. Awards subject to review.
8: With costs and funding plans laid out: how do we deliver the robot?
Admin, across all groups: fundraising, sponsors, purchasing and competition logistics.
Design & build: chassis, gimbal and feeder; fabrication, assembly and mechanical tests.
Electronics: power, motor controllers and referee hardware; interface and cutoff tests.
Software: manual control and system communication; then camera capture and possible vision assistance.
Three technical groups work in parallel and combine their work throughout the build.
Shared result: drive, aim and fire with a working referee system.
Next: the people leading each group.
13: Now, general membership: open participation across all four groups.
Beginners: defined tasks and guidance. Experienced members: larger subsystem responsibilities.
FRC and VEX graduates: a natural transition from high-school to university robotics.
Recruit from that experience in building, programming and competing.
Experienced members help newcomers through shared projects and guidance.
Each lead assigns work, supports members and reviews progress.
Responsibility grows with skills and commitment, keeping open membership tied to delivery.
14: Given those groups and recruitment plans: here is the path to competition.
Key target: working robot by March, leaving time to test, qualify and practise.
September–October: funding, orders, chassis and parts list; software recruitment.
November–January: rolling chassis and launcher tests; motor/power bench tests; validated motor-control software.
February–March: combine gimbal, feeder, mounts, referee system, cutoff and drive/aim/fire software.
April onward: qualification evidence, compliance checks, match tests and fault fixes.
May–June: pilot training, spares, repair practice and transport.
Dates depend on the event schedule; protect time for testing rather than rushing before competition.
15: Finally, safety: start with the projectile — 3.2 g at 25 m/s.
Then compare with Duma’s eye-impact study: roughly 3× its 50% corneal-abrasion benchmark.
Implication: direct eye impact is an injury hazard.
Contain testing in UTRA Combat’s wooden box, after confirming it contains shots.
Outside the enclosure: everyone present wears impact-rated safety goggles.
Pair these controls with mandatory UTRA safety training before hands-on work.
Training: safe testing, emergency stops, disabling and unloading before access.
